title: Listening in Bairari
hook: a tiny raga, a few hymns, easy to hear whole

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bairari, whose first hymn says sun man, listen, mind, and your line was small and bright. What small thing did you really see? Day one thousand ninety-one.

The Guru Granth Sahib is easy to meet in pieces. One shabad in the morning. A hukamnama, the day's reading opened at random. A few lines sung in kirtan, then the next raga, the next Guru, the next page. A book this large invites that. Bairari offers something different: a whole section you can take in at once, beginning to end, without losing the thread. A few hymns, a short stretch of pages, and then it's done. Today: listening in Bairari, all of it.
screen: `USUALLY IN PIECES.` → `ONE SHABAD, ONE HUKAMNAMA.` → `A WHOLE SECTION AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the walk through it. It begins where yesterday left off, with Guru Ram Das: sun man, listen, mind, to the untellable story of the Lord's Name. Then more of his hymns follow, turning the same light around. One of them has a refrain worth carrying out of the room. It opens: har jan ram naam gun gaavai. In paraphrase: the Lord's servant sings the praises of the Name; and if anyone slanders that servant, the servant doesn't lose their own goodness. Sit with that for a second. Slander is aimed at someone, but in this refrain it can't take anything from them. The goodness stays where it was. Then the voice changes. Guru Arjan, mahala five, closes the section, and his hymn moves from the single listener to a crowd: in paraphrase, the saints met together and sang the Lord's praise, and the pains of countless lifetimes went away. Hear the whole arc. A mind told to listen. A servant who can't be robbed of goodness by someone else's words. And a gathering, singing together. One person, then a person under pressure, then a sangat. That's a shape you only notice when you hear the section whole. Read one hymn and you get a line. Read all of Bairari and you get a little journey from listening alone to singing together. Today's line: the whole of it. And tomorrow, Raga Tilang, the next section, where the colors change again.
screen: `FIRST: LISTEN, MIND.` · `SLANDER CAN'T TAKE THE GOODNESS.` · `GURU ARJAN: THE SAINTS SING TOGETHER.` · `ALONE, UNDER PRESSURE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE OF IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to all of it. If you have a Gurbani app or a printed Granth with meanings, open it to the Bairari pages and read straight through, slowly, without skipping. If you can find recordings, play the Bairari shabads one after another. Then sit, and let the whole arc settle: listening, steadiness, singing together. Don't pick a favorite line yet. Just hold the shape of it, start to finish, the way you'd hold a short letter after reading it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you reach the end. The bell holds the time.
Listening in Bairari. The short raga heard whole: a mind told to listen, a servant slander can't rob, and the saints singing together. Today's word.
Your line: the whole of it. Today, finish one small thing all the way through, a song, a chapter, a conversation, without skipping to the end or splitting your attention. Day one thousand ninety-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Granth in daily shabads, in the hukamnama read at random each day, and in kirtan; some also read whole sections or the whole Granth through, and a short raga like Bairari can be read in one sitting.

notes: All three hymns are paraphrased. Please confirm 'Har jan ram naam gun gaavai / je koi nind kare har jan ki apuna gun na gavaavai' is in Bairari Mahala 4 (Ang 719) and the paraphrase is fair.

Please confirm that Guru Arjan's single Bairari hymn is 'Sant jana mil har jas gaaio' (Ang 720), that it closes the section, and that 'the pains of countless lifetimes went away' fairly renders it ('kot janam ke dookh', given without a number).
The hook's 'easy to meet in pieces' and howItsDone's 'some also read whole sections' describe general practice without counts; please confirm.
